mentions.author: Donna Haraway
mentions.section: Introduction: Why Data Science Needs Feminism
mentions.before: Each of the following chapters takes up one of these principles, drawing upon examples from the field of data science, expansively defined, to show how that principle can be put into action.
mentions.sentence: Along the way, we introduce key feminist concepts like the matrix of domination (Patricia Hill Collins; see chapter 1), situated knowledge (Donna Haraway; see chapter 3), and emotional labor (Arlie Hochschild; see chapter 8), as well as some of our own ideas about what data feminism looks like in theory and practice.
mentions.after: To this end, we introduce you to people at the cutting edge of data and justice.

mentions.author: Safiya Umoja Noble

mentions.after: Noble describes how, as recently as 2016, comparable searches for “three Black teenagers” and “three white teenagers” turned up wildly different representations of those teens.

mentions.after: So is a diverse database of faces really a good idea?

mentions.author: Virginia Eubanks
mentions.before: This results in women, people of color, and poor people, among others, being overrepresented in the data that these systems are premised upon.
mentions.sentence: In Automating Inequality, for example, Virginia Eubanks tells the story of the Allegheny County Office of Children, Youth, and Families in western Pennsylvania, which employs an algorithmic model to predict the risk of child abuse in any particular home.
mentions.after: The goal of the model is to remove children from potentially abusive households before it happens; this would appear to be a very worthy goal.

mentions.author: Virginia Eubanks
mentions.before: The goal of the model is to remove children from potentially abusive households before it happens; this would appear to be a very worthy goal.
mentions.sentence: As Eubanks shows, however, inequities result.
mentions.after: For wealthier parents, who can more easily access private health care and mental health services, there is simply not that much data to pull into the model.

mentions.author: Virginia Eubanks
mentions.before: Because there are far more data about poor parents, they are oversampled in the model, and so their children are overtargeted as being at risk for child abuse—a risk that results in children being removed from their families and homes.
mentions.sentence: Eubanks argues that the model “confuse[s] parenting while poor with poor parenting.”
mentions.after: This model, like many, was designed under two flawed assumptions: (1) that more data is always better and (2) that the data are a neutral input.

mentions.author: Virginia Eubanks
mentions.before: Viewed from the perspective of the state, there were simply not enough employees to handle all of the potential child abuse cases, so it needed a mechanism for efficiently deploying limited staff—or so the reasoning goes.
mentions.sentence: This is what Eubanks has described as a scarcity bias: the idea that there are not enough resources for everyone so we should think small and allow technology to fill the gaps.
mentions.after: Such thinking, and the technological “solutions” that result, often meet the goals of their creators—in this case, the Allegheny County Office of Children, Youth, and Families—but not the goals of the children and families that it purports to serve.

mentions.author: Ruha Benjamin
mentions.before: Courtesy of Julia Angwin, Jeff Larson, Surya Mattu, and Lauren Kirchner for ProPublica, 2016.
mentions.sentence: Sociologist Ruha Benjamin has a term for these situations: the New Jim Code —where software code and a false sense of objectivity come together to contain and control the lives of Black people, and of other people of color.
mentions.after: In this regard, the redlining map and the Equivant risk assessment algorithm share some additional similarities.

mentions.author: Ruha Benjamin
mentions.before: Envision Equity, Imagine Co-liberation As the examples discussed thus far in this book clearly demonstrate, one of the most dangerous outcomes of the tools of data and data science being consolidated in the hands of dominant groups is that these groups are able to obscure their politics and their goals behind their technologies.
mentions.sentence: Benjamin, whose book Race after Technology: Abolitionist Tools for the New Jim Code (mentioned earlier), describes this phenomenon as the “imagined objectivity of data and technology” because data-driven systems like redlining and risk assessment algorithms are not really objective at all.
mentions.after: Her concept of imagined objectivity emphasizes the role that cultural assumptions and personal preconceptions play in upholding this false belief: one imagines (wrongly) that datasets and algorithms are less partial and less discriminatory than people and thus more “objective.”

mentions.author: Ruha Benjamin
mentions.before: This is a promising development, especially for technical fields that have not historically foregrounded ethical issues, and as funding mechanisms for research on data and ethics proliferate.
mentions.sentence: However, as Benjamin’s concept of imagined objectivity helps to show, addressing bias in a dataset is a tiny technological Band-Aid for a much larger problem.
mentions.after: Even the values mentioned here, which seek to address instances of bias in data-driven systems, are themselves non-neutral, as they locate the source of the bias in individual people and specific design decisions.

mentions.author: Sasha Costanza-Chock
mentions.before: In contrast, the concepts on the right start from the basic feminist belief that oppression is real, historic, ongoing, and worth dismantling.
mentions.sentence: Media theorist and designer Sasha Costanza-Chock proposes a restorative approach to data justice.
mentions.after: Drawing from theories of restorative justice—meaning that decisions should be made in ways that recognize and rectify any harms of the past—Costanza-Chock asserts that any notion of algorithmic fairness must also acknowledge the systematic nature of the unfairness that has long been perpetrated by certain groups on others.

mentions.author: Sasha Costanza-Chock
mentions.before: Media theorist and designer Sasha Costanza-Chock proposes a restorative approach to data justice.
mentions.sentence: Drawing from theories of restorative justice—meaning that decisions should be made in ways that recognize and rectify any harms of the past—Costanza-Chock asserts that any notion of algorithmic fairness must also acknowledge the systematic nature of the unfairness that has long been perpetrated by certain groups on others.
mentions.after: They give the example of college admissions—a topic that always seems to be in the news, not the least because it’s a major mechanism of protecting privilege.

mentions.author: Sasha Costanza-Chock
mentions.before: If you are a Black woman or a Muslim man or a transgender service member and you live in the United States today, your being in the world is political, whether or not you want it to be.
mentions.sentence: So rather than design algorithms that purport to be “color-blind” (since color-blindness is of course a myth), Costanza-Chock explains that we should be designing algorithms that are just.
mentions.after: This means shifting from the ahistorical notion of fairness to a model of equity.

mentions.author: Virginia Eubanks
mentions.before: This difficulty also underscores the point that bias (in individuals, in datasets, in statistical models, or in algorithms) is not a strong enough concept in which to anchor ideas about equity and justice.
mentions.sentence: In writing about the creation of New York’s Welfare Management System in the early 1970s, for example, Virginia Eubanks describes: “These early big data systems were built on a specific understanding of what constitutes discrimination: personal bias.”
mentions.after: The solution at the time was to remove the humans from the loop, and it remains so today: without potentially bad—in this case, racist—apples, there would be less discrimination.

mentions.author: Virginia Eubanks
mentions.before: But this line of thinking illustrates what whiteness studies scholar Robin DiAngelo would call the new racism: the belief that racism is due to individual bad actors, rather than structures or systems.
mentions.sentence: In relation to welfare management, Eubanks emphasizes that this often meant replacing social workers, who were often women of color, and who had empathy and flexibility and listening skills, with an automated system that applies a set of rigid criteria, no matter what the circumstances.
mentions.after: While bias remains a serious problem, it should not be viewed as something that can be fixed after the fact.

mentions.author: Donna Haraway
mentions.before: There is no such thing as mastery of feminism because those who hold positions of privilege—like those in data science, like the Local Lotto course designers, and like us, the authors of this book—are constantly learning how to be better allies and accomplices across difference.
mentions.sentence: In this process, what becomes most important is to “stay with the trouble,” as feminist philosopher Donna Haraway would say.
mentions.after: Staying with the trouble means persisting in your work, especially when it becomes uncomfortable, unclear, or outright upsetting.

mentions.author: Donna Haraway
mentions.section: Chapter 3: On Rational, Scientific, Objective Viewpoints from Mythical, Imaginary, Impossible Standpoints
mentions.before: At a data visualization master class in 2013, workshop leaders from the Guardian newspaper held up spreadsheet data—spreadsheet data!—as an ideal for the communication of quantitative data, calling it: “Clarity without persuasion.”
mentions.sentence: But persuasion is everywhere, even in spreadsheets, and—as feminist philosopher Donna Haraway would likely argue—especially in spreadsheets.
mentions.after: In the 1980s, Haraway was among the first to connect the seeming neutrality and objectivity of data and their visual display to the ideas about distance that we’ve just discussed.

mentions.author: Donna Haraway
mentions.section: Chapter 3: On Rational, Scientific, Objective Viewpoints from Mythical, Imaginary, Impossible Standpoints
mentions.before: But persuasion is everywhere, even in spreadsheets, and—as feminist philosopher Donna Haraway would likely argue—especially in spreadsheets.
mentions.sentence: In the 1980s, Haraway was among the first to connect the seeming neutrality and objectivity of data and their visual display to the ideas about distance that we’ve just discussed.
mentions.after: She described data visualization, in particular, as “the god trick of seeing everything from nowhere.”

mentions.author: Donna Haraway
mentions.section: Chapter 3: On Rational, Scientific, Objective Viewpoints from Mythical, Imaginary, Impossible Standpoints
mentions.before: It’s also the most ethically complicated to navigate for the ways in which it masks the people, the methods, the questions, and the messiness that lies behind clean lines and geometric shapes.
mentions.sentence: Haraway calls it the god trick: it’s a trick because it makes the viewer believe that they can see everything, all at once, from an imaginary and impossible standpoint.
mentions.after: But it’s also a trick because what appears to be everything, and what appears to be neutral, is always what she terms a partial perspective.

mentions.author: Donna Haraway
mentions.section: Chapter 3: On Rational, Scientific, Objective Viewpoints from Mythical, Imaginary, Impossible Standpoints
mentions.before: (We discuss this more in chapter 4.)
mentions.sentence: For now, the important thing to note is how false binaries work to benefit a single one of Haraway’s partial perspectives: that of the group already at the top—elite white men.
mentions.after: How can we let go of this binary logic?

mentions.author: Donna Haraway
mentions.section: Chapter 3: On Rational, Scientific, Objective Viewpoints from Mythical, Imaginary, Impossible Standpoints
mentions.before: Rather than valorizing the neutrality ideal and trying to expunge all human traces from a data product because of their bias, feminist philosophers have proposed a goal of more complete knowledge.
mentions.sentence: Donna Haraway’s idea of the god trick comes from a larger argument about the importance of developing feminist objectivity.
mentions.after: It’s not just data visualization but all forms of knowledge that are situated, she explains, meaning that they are produced by specific people in specific circumstances—cultural, historical, and geographic.

mentions.author: Donna Haraway
mentions.section: Chapter 3: On Rational, Scientific, Objective Viewpoints from Mythical, Imaginary, Impossible Standpoints
mentions.before: Feminist objectivity is a tool that can account for the situated nature of knowledge and can bring together multiple—what she terms partial —perspectives.
mentions.sentence: Sandra Harding, who developed her ideas alongside Haraway, proposes a concept of strong objectivity.
mentions.after: This form of objectivity works toward more inclusive knowledge production by centering the perspectives—or standpoints —of groups that are otherwise excluded from knowledge-making processes.

mentions.author: Donna Haraway
mentions.section: Chapter 3: On Rational, Scientific, Objective Viewpoints from Mythical, Imaginary, Impossible Standpoints
mentions.before: The key to fixing this problem is to acknowledge that all science, and indeed all work in the world, is undertaken by individuals.
mentions.sentence: Each person occupies a particular perspective, as Haraway might say; a particular standpoint, as Harding might say; or a particular set of positionalities, as Alcott might say.
mentions.after: And all would agree that research by only men and about only men cannot be universalized to make knowledge claims about all other people in the world.

mentions.author: Sasha Costanza-Chock
mentions.before: Or, consider another person with a history of bad experiences at the (literal) hands of the TSA.
mentions.sentence: Sasha Costanza-Chock is nonbinary, like Maria Munir.
mentions.after: They are also a design professor at MIT, so they have a lot of experience both living with and thinking through oppressive classification systems.

mentions.author: Sasha Costanza-Chock
mentions.before: (And while we’re going down that path, how about we imagine a future without a state agency that systematically pathologizes Black women and trans people and Cub Scouts in the first place?)
mentions.sentence: So when we say that what gets counted counts, it’s folks like Sasha Costanza-Chock or Mikey Hicks or Maria Munir that we’re thinking about.
mentions.after: Because flawed classification systems—like the one that underlies the airport scanner’s risk-detection algorithm or the one that determines which names end up on terrorist watch lists or simply (simply!) the gender binary—are not only significant problems in themselves, but also symptoms of a more global condition of inequality.

mentions.author: Donna Haraway
mentions.section: Chapter 5: Unicorns, Janitors, Ninjas, Wizards, and Rock Stars
mentions.before: This goal reflects a key tenet of feminist thinking, which is the recognition that a multiplicity of voices, rather than one single loud or technical or magical one, results in a more complete picture of the issue at hand.
mentions.sentence: Feminist philosophers like Donna Haraway, who we introduced in chapter 3, prompted a wave of thinkers who have continued to develop the idea that all knowledge is partial, meaning no single person or group can claim an objective view of the capital-T Truth.
mentions.after: But embracing pluralism, as this concept is often described today, does not mean that everything is relative, nor does it mean that all truth claims have equal weight.

mentions.author: Donna Haraway
mentions.section: Chapter 6: The Numbers Don’t Speak for Themselves
mentions.before: And this lack of context becomes even more of a liability when accompanied by the kind of marketing hype we see in GDELT and other Big Dick Data projects.
mentions.sentence: In fact, the 1980s version of these claims is what led Donna Haraway to propose the concept of situated knowledge in the first place.
mentions.after: Subsequent feminist work has drawn on the concept of situated knowledge to elaborate ideas about ethics and responsibility in relation to knowledge-making.

mentions.author: Safiya Umoja Noble
mentions.section: Chapter 6: The Numbers Don’t Speak for Themselves
mentions.before: But what happens when the number of links is also highly correlated with sexist, racist, and pornographic results?
mentions.sentence: The influence of racism, sexism, and colonialism is precisely what we see described in Algorithms of Oppression, information studies scholar Safiya Umoja Noble’s study of the harmful stereotypes about Black and Latinx women perpetuated by search algorithms such as Google’s.
mentions.after: As discussed in chapter 1, Noble demonstrates that Google Search results do not simply correlate with our racist, sexist, and colonialist society; that society causes the racist and sexist results.

mentions.before: The influence of racism, sexism, and colonialism is precisely what we see described in Algorithms of Oppression, information studies scholar Safiya Umoja Noble’s study of the harmful stereotypes about Black and Latinx women perpetuated by search algorithms such as Google’s.
mentions.sentence: As discussed in chapter 1, Noble demonstrates that Google Search results do not simply correlate with our racist, sexist, and colonialist society; that society causes the racist and sexist results.
mentions.after: More than that, Google Search reinforces these oppressive views by ranking results according to how many other sites link to them.

mentions.author: Sara Ahmed
mentions.before: Crediting Data Work The emphasis on giving formal credit for a broad range of work derives from feminist practices of citation.
mentions.sentence: Feminist theorist Sara Ahmed describes this practice as a way of resisting how certain types of people—usually cis and white and male—“take up spaces by screening out others.”
mentions.after: When those other people are screened out, they become invisible, and their contributions go unrecognized.

mentions.author: Sara Ahmed
mentions.before: When those other people are screened out, they become invisible, and their contributions go unrecognized.
mentions.sentence: The screening techniques that lead to their erasure, as Ahmed terms them, are not always intentional, but they are, unfortunately, self-perpetuating.
mentions.after: Ahmed gives the example of sinking into a leather armchair that is comfortable because it’s molded to the shape of your body over time.

mentions.author: Sara Ahmed
mentions.before: The screening techniques that lead to their erasure, as Ahmed terms them, are not always intentional, but they are, unfortunately, self-perpetuating.
mentions.sentence: Ahmed gives the example of sinking into a leather armchair that is comfortable because it’s molded to the shape of your body over time.
mentions.after: You probably wouldn’t notice how the chair would be uncomfortable for those who haven’t spent time sitting in it—those with different bodies or with different demands on their time.

mentions.author: Ruha Benjamin
mentions.before: But in more instances than you might think, the labor associated with data work can be surfaced through the data themselves.
mentions.sentence: For instance, historian Benjamin Schmidt, whose research centers on the role of government agencies in shaping public knowledge, decided to visualize the metadata associated with the digital catalog of the US Library of Congress, the largest library in the world (figure 7.7).
mentions.after: Schmidt’s initial goal was to understand the collection and the classification system that structured the catalog.

mentions.author: Mar Hicks
mentions.before: Although the Google Walkout for Real Change, as the protest was formally known, was framed in the media as a milestone for big tech, there are clear precedents for white-collar tech organizing.
mentions.sentence: Historian Mar Hicks has connected the Google walkout to a strike among computer workers—then a workforce that was comprised mainly of women—that took place in the United Kingdom in the 1970s.
mentions.after: The strike took down twenty-six government computer centers and disrupted the work of nine others.

mentions.author: Mar Hicks
mentions.before: The government was required to pay attention.
mentions.sentence: Writes Hicks, “Even though many of these workers were women, and limited in their pay, promotion, and work opportunities due to sexism, their proximity to the literal machinery of government gave them a great deal of power.”
mentions.after: The organizers of the Google walkout recognized their proximity to another source of power: Google itself.

mentions.author: Sasha Costanza-Chock
mentions.before: Some groups are using movement-building strategies to effect change across entire industries.
mentions.sentence: For example, Una Lee, Wesley Taylor, Victoria Barnett, Ebony Dumas, Carlos (L05) Garcia, and Sasha Costanza-Chock are coordinating a networked community of practice called design justice.
mentions.after: The idea for design justice emerged from a workshop at the Allied Media Conference in Detroit in 2015, where thirty people assembled to challenge the idea of “design for good.”
